speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: asked the Prime Minister in light of rising interest rates (a) whether there has been an increasing trend over the past year in the number of financially-distressed consumers who have sought debt management assistance; (b) whether the Government intends to introduce measures to afford temporary respite to consumers and businesses who encounter short-term liquidity issues; and (c) what are some foreseeable knock-on impacts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: And the Monetary Authority of Singapore's (MAS) stress test suggests that the median household's mortgage servicing ratio should remain manageable, even under scenarios of significantly higher interest rates or lower incomes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Here, too, MAS' stress test suggests that debt servicing of Singapore-listed firms is likely to remain manageable as interest rates rise, with most firms having sufficient earnings to cover their interest expenses and cash reserves to provide buffers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Industry-wide credit relief measures have been gradually withdrawn, in line with the broadening of the economic recovery and the steady decline in the number of applications for assistance.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: These measures, introduced in March 2020, were meant to provide short-term relief and support to individuals and SMEs, as stringent public health measures led to temporary cashflow difficulties.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Conversely, recent market-driven interest rate increases have been accompanied by continuing income growth.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: This mitigates their impact on the debt-servicing ability of most borrowers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Indeed, the debt relief schemes introduced during the pandemic are not meant to insulate borrowers from the normalisation of interest rates.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: However, a small segment of households, especially those with higher leverages, could be more constrained by higher interest rates.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: So, they should approach their lenders early to explore possible loan refinancing and repayment solutions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: For financially-distressed HDB homeowners, MAS has worked with MND, HDB, MOM and financial institutions to establish standardised interventions when late repayments occur.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: These include potential loan restructuring solutions, early referrals to appropriate social service agencies and, in certain limited cases, helping them obtain alternative HDB accommodation where foreclosures are unavoidable.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Likewise, companies with low net profit margins should approach their lenders early to work out suitable loan repayment schemes and plans.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: More broadly, everyone should exercise caution in their new borrowings.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Households and businesses should plan for future and further interest rate increases and be sure of their ability to service their loans before making additional long-term financial commitments.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: First, the reason why I am asking this question is because I am concerned about the slow, but then, eventually, rapid boil from the rising interest rates, in particular, the impact on the rising cash outlays by households and businesses, particularly from the cascading effect of the interest rate.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, my first question: is it possible to assess the rising cash outflows and its impact on households from the rising interest rates for this year and next?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The second question is probably what is the proportion of Singaporean households vulnerable and likely to turn vulnerable at the margin, rather than currently vulnerable, as mentioned by the Minister of State.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And what can they do now as Singaporean households and businesses mostly affected by the potentially slow, but then, rapidly boiling effects of rising interest rates, as we go forward beyond the second half of this year?

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Most households should still be able to service their mortgages and other debt obligations, as Singapore's domestic interest rates pick up alongside global rates.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The total debt servicing ratio framework (TDSR) captures a borrower's monthly expenses on all types of debt, including mortgages, car loans and unsecured debt, as a proportion of income.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The overall debt servicing ability of households has, thus far, remained manageable, with the median TDSR being 43% last year.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: This is well within the recently tightened TDSR threshold of 55%.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: So, 43% median TDSR last year and the tightened TDSR threshold at 55%.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: But, beyond mortgages, MAS has also imposed rules for car loans, as well as unsecured credit, to encourage prudent borrowing.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: This has helped the credit profile across these consumer loan products to remain healthy.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The proportion of credit card rollover balances, as a share of GDP, for example, has declined since the pre-pandemic period from 1.3% in Q4 2019, to about 1% as at end 2021, and the charge-off rates have similarly decreased from 6.3% in Q4 2019, to 4.4% as at end 2021.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: In addition, only 0.01% of borrowers have defaulted on car loans granted by financial institutions, as at end 2021.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: For the Member's second question on what consumers can do, I think that, generally, consumers can seek assistance for their outstanding debt.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: For example, consumers in financial distress can seek help from Credit Counselling Singapore for debt management assistance or consider taking up commercial products, such as debt consolidation plans, that may alleviate their repayment burdens.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Consumers, borrowers, members of the public can go on to MoneySense.gov.sg – that is a website that we continue to build at MAS – to help consumers understand their credit profiles, what kind of products are available on the market and also to exercise prudence in their borrowing, particularly in an environment of heightened interest rates.
